newsitem.title: USA: U.S. steelmakers seen facing consolidation hurdles. [CORRECTED 06:39 GMT 05/04]
newsitem.headline: U.S. steelmakers seen facing consolidation hurdles. [CORRECTED 06:39 GMT 05/04]

text.p: (Corrects by removing quote in second paragraph.)

A consolidation of the U.S. steel industry is necessary to strengthen its profitability, but large mergers could prove difficult for companies saddled with high health-care and pension costs, analysts said on Friday.

Still, analysts said steel executives appeared to be taking action to address the problem of overcapacity, as reflected in comments this week by U.S. Steel President Paul Wilhelm. He said his company was scouting prospects for possible mergers or acquisitions.

Wall Street has long held that Big Steel has too many players serving a handful of large customers, including the major U.S. automakers, General Motors Corp, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp. At least a half dozen U.S. steelmakers supply the automakers and other large customers, such as appliance manufacturers.
Because of oversupply, customers often have the upper hand in contract negotiations and have been able to keep a lid on prices. That in turn has depressed earnings for steelmakers.

"(Customers) are in a substantially better position when it comes to pricing than the steel industry," said Chuck Bradford at UBS Securities. "The industry has done a good job of cutting costs, but they're not going to get to a satisfactory level of profitability with just cutting costs. They need to consolidate."

Wilhelm, speaking at an analysts' meeting on Wednesday, said options for U.S. Steel -- the largest U.S. steelmaker and the world's eighth biggest -- could include merging with a large rival, such as Inland Steel Industries Inc or National Steel Corp.
A spokesman for Inland Steel declined to comment. Officials from National Steel were unavailable.

Even though speculation that U.S. Steel would merge with a competitor has circulated for years, analysts said the company -- and some of its rivals -- now seemed more open to the possibililty of consolidation than in the past.
One reason they might be more receptive, analysts said, is increased capacity from upstart minimills that have come on line recently or will do so in the coming months.

"The thinking seems to be moving from theoretical to active," said Richard Aldrich at Lehman Brothers. "I think (executives) are starting to say, 'Let's talk and do some work and see how the pieces will fit together.'"

A spokesman said U.S. Steel had no plans currently. "We're always willing to look at options to improve shareholder value. That can include other companies or expanding operations. Nothing is hot, nothing is imminent," he said.

Still, analysts said Wilhelm's comments could signal that the industry, which has had no merger activity in at least a decade, may be poised to move in that direction. The three other major U.S. steelmakers are AK Steel Holding Corp, Bethlehem Steel Corp and LTV Corp.
"It's definitely a positive sign, that (U.S. Steel) recognizes the need for consolidation. It has to happen," Gambardella said.

But analysts said many steel companies, after undergoing downsizing in the 1980s and finding themselves saddled with so-called "legacy" costs, including health care and pensions, may not make attractive acquisition targets. Legacy costs are assumed after plant shutdowns and job layoffs.
"The steel industry, as a generalization, is saddled with large legacy liabilities," Aldrich said. He suggested U.S. Steel might instead buy a piece of a competitor or a steel distribution business.
Analysts said they expected some sort of merger in the industry in the next year or two.

"I think the odds are certainly better that by sometime in '98 you're going to see some activity," Aldrich said. "The question is, how do you do it without making your company more financially weak in terms of the balance sheet."
